opportunities.title: Front-door and document-chase agent for tax season (intake -> consult -> engagement -> evidence collected)
opportunities.problem: Every prospect and every client enters through one of two unautomated channels - a POST-back web form with no booking and no stated response time, or a single phone line answered alongside billable work - and then the firm has to collect documents from that client over weeks, reconciling a TaxDome request link against a still-live legacy ShareFile link. With two principals and no visible intake coordinator, the inbound email address is the lead principal's own, so call-backs and chase cycles compete directly with return preparation and SOC 1 fieldwork.
evidence: Consultation intake is a static form (name, phone, email, company, free-text) that posts back to consultation.htm, plus a sidebar duplicate form on interior pages; no calendar or booking mechanism exists anywhere on the site (https://www.rizickcpas.com/consultation.htm)

The only alternative to the form is the main number 732-387-0872, and the published general email is the lead principal's (gail@rizickcpas.com); no business hours or after-hours path is published (https://www.rizickcpas.com/contact.htm)

Client file exchange runs through a TaxDome file-request link while the site header still carries an older ShareFile link - two overlapping document systems (https://www.rizickcpas.com/consultation.htm)

Workload is deadline-clustered across 1040/1065/1120/trust and estate returns with e-filing, alongside SOC 1 Type 2 examinations that require evidence collected across an audit period (https://www.rizickcpas.com/income-tax-preparation-services.htm)

Clients specifically praise being walked through what documents to deliver and emailing documents remotely, i.e. the collection step is the client-facing interaction the firm is judged on (https://www.rizickcpas.com/testimonials.htm)
Structural seasonality is an industry norm: 55% of tax preparers report seasonal work schedules and 38% face time pressure every day (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/13-2082.00)
opportunities.agent_design: An event-driven intake-and-collection agent sits in front of the existing site form and mailbox. (1) On each form submission or inbound email it classifies the request (individual return, business return, SOC 1, valuation, bookkeeping), drafts a reply with the correct document checklist and two or three offered consult slots, and opens a record in a lightweight pipeline the firm can see. (2) On engagement it creates the TaxDome file request from the checklist for that return type, then runs a scheduled chase loop (day 3/7/14, then weekly) that references exactly which items are still missing, and escalates stalled items to a human queue. (3) It reads inbound attachments and portal uploads, marks checklist items satisfied, and flags mismatches (wrong year, password-protected file, missing statement page) before a person opens anything. (4) A daily digest gives each principal a ranked list of returns blocked on the client. Human approval gates: scope and fee quotes, any reply to a new prospect the agent cannot classify with confidence, and every outbound message that states tax advice or a filing deadline extension. Systems touched: website form handler, firm mailbox, TaxDome portal, an internal status table; QuickBooks only for existing-client lookup if the firm exposes it.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: A chatbot subscription cannot hold per-client state across 150+ returns, cannot trigger a 21-day chase sequence, cannot read portal uploads and reconcile them against a per-return checklist, and cannot reconcile two document systems. It also cannot enforce the firm's confidentiality obligations: IRC Sec. 7216 restricts disclosing return information to third parties without consent, and the FTC Safeguards Rule treats tax preparation firms as financial institutions requiring contracted service providers, MFA and encryption - so the agent has to run on a vetted deployment with logging and consent handling, not a consumer AI tool with tax data pasted into it.

impact_estimate.range: $3,000-$12,000 per year of recovered admin and principal hours (roughly 80-200 hours)
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assumes 100-250 active individual/business clients and 2-4 document exchanges per return; that intake triage plus chasing and status upkeep currently consumes 6-10 hrs/week from January to mid-April and 2-3 hrs/week in the remaining months (~170-275 hrs/yr); and that automation removes 40-60% of that time. Hours valued at a blended $36-$62/hr: NJ bookkeeping-clerk median $58,300/yr (~$28/hr base) for the chase/status portion, rising toward the NJ accountant median $100,830/yr (~$48/hr base) for principal review time. Range excludes any revenue from faster lead response, which the profile does not quantify.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2-4 weeks: connect the website form and one mailbox; build three document checklists (1040, 1065/1120, SOC 1 evidence); run the chase loop on live new engagements for one cohort plus a dry-run backfill over last season's stalled files; deliver a daily blocked-returns digest and a measured before/after count of chase emails and days-to-complete-documents for that cohort.

opportunities.title: SOC 1 evidence intake and control-testing workpaper pipeline
opportunities.problem: SOC 1 Type 1 and Type 2 examinations are the firm's most defensible, highest-value line, but each Type 2 requires assembling and testing control evidence across a whole audit period - population listings, sample selections, screen captures, review sign-offs - and then tracing every tested attribute into a workpaper. For a two-principal firm this is the task most likely to be done late at night and the one most likely to cap how many examinations the firm can accept in a season.
evidence: The firm performs SSAE 18 examinations and issues SOC 1 Type 1 (description) and Type 2 (description plus testing) reports, with example clients such as 401(k) recordkeepers and third-party administrators (https://www.rizickcpas.com/soc1-audits.htm)
Type 2 work requires evidence collection and testing across an audit period, i.e. recurring document gathering rather than a single year-end file (https://www.rizickcpas.com/soc1-audits.htm)

A 150-person regional CPA firm reports a 30-60% reduction in associate time on audit evidence review after an OCR-plus-LLM deployment, against a baseline of roughly 1,900 hours per associate per year (single-firm self-report, no control group - treated as the optimistic bound) (https://www.peasebell.com/insights/what-happens-in-vegas/)

A vendor case study reports Johnson Lambert cutting time per financial-risk audit from 60-80 hours to 12-16 hours by building a document-to-structure pipeline, with staff shifted from tie-outs to document review (vendor-reported, rated Low) (https://provectus.com/case-studies/johnson-lambert-audit/)

Attest conclusions must remain traceable to cited source evidence and be signed by a licensed professional; a practitioner account notes the standards 'still apply in full' despite automation (https://www.peasebell.com/insights/what-happens-in-vegas/)
opportunities.agent_design: An internal workpaper pipeline rather than a chat interface. (1) An ingestion step pulls the client's control evidence bundle (PDFs, screenshots, exports) from the portal and OCRs it, assigning each document to a control and a tested attribute using a firm-defined control matrix. (2) A document-extraction agent pulls the tested values (who performed the review, date, ticket ID, exception count) and compares them to the sample selection and to the prior period, then drafts the test-of-control workpaper row with a citation to the page and bounding box it read. (3) A completeness agent reconciles the evidence received against the sample list and produces a missing-evidence request the engagement lead can send in one click. (4) An exception agent flags gaps, out-of-period items and inconsistent sign-offs into a review queue rather than concluding anything. Human approval: every exception disposition, every conclusion and the final report are made by the licensed principal; the agent only assembles and cites. Everything runs in a private/isolated environment because client control evidence is confidential.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: This is not a writing assistant - it needs a control-to-attribute data model, OCR of scanned and screenshot evidence, a reconciliation of received items against a sample list, per-client isolation and a full citation trail for AICPA peer review. Off-the-shelf chatbots hallucinate citations, cannot be audited, and cannot be pointed at client control evidence without breaching confidentiality and the FTC Safeguards service-provider requirements. The firm's public 2024 peer review also means documentation quality is externally inspected, so traceability is a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have.

impact_estimate.range: $2,000-$12,000 per year of staff hours (roughly 40-180 hours), plus capacity for about one additional Type 2 engagement
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assumes 2-5 SOC 1 engagements per year at 60-140 hours each of evidence handling, tie-out and workpaper drafting (150-600 hours; engagement count and hours are not published, so this is an inference from a 3-8 person firm doing Type 1 and Type 2 work). Applies only a 15-30% reduction, well below the 30-60% single-firm self-report and the 60-80 to 12-16 hour vendor claim, because a small firm has less volume to amortize tooling over. Hours valued at $48-$65/hr (NJ accountant median $100,830/yr base, plus burden). Added engagement capacity is stated as capacity, not dollars, because the firm publishes no fees.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2-4 weeks: pick one in-flight or most recent SOC 1 Type 2 engagement and one control family; build the control matrix and OCR ingestion; produce draft workpaper rows with page-level citations and a missing-evidence list for the next client request; measure hours per control against the engagement lead's own estimate. No conclusions are generated in the pilot.

opportunities.title: Firm knowledge agent over the content library, checklists and prior-year answers
opportunities.problem: The firm's differentiator in its own testimonials is explaining returns clearly and being easy to reach, and it already publishes hundreds of tax and accounting articles - but that content sits on a static marketing site disconnected from the practice. Meanwhile the same recurring questions (what documents do I need, why did my refund change, which states do I file in, what does a SOC 1 report cover) are answered by a principal or a staff member, in season, one at a time, and not at all after hours since no hours or after-hours path are published.
evidence: The firm publishes a Content Library of 'hundreds' of tax and accounting articles across 10 categories plus a newsletter, Tax Center and Tax Tips pages - a large, firm-authored knowledge base that is not connected to any answering tool (https://www.rizickcpas.com/content_library.htm)

Clients cite explanation quality and year-round planning as the reason they stay - summary sheets explaining each part of the return, multi-state returns handled (https://www.rizickcpas.com/testimonials.htm)
No chat widget, no FAQ bot and no client-status feature exists on the site; it is static HTML with no CMS (https://www.rizickcpas.com/sitemap.xml)
No business hours and no after-hours contact path are published, so off-hours questions have nowhere to go (https://www.rizickcpas.com/contact.htm)

Adjacent evidence: a generative-AI assistant deployed to 5,179 support agents raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average and by 34% for novices, though this is structured knowledge work rather than accounting-specific; the Stanford field study of 79 small and mid-sized accounting firms reports 55% higher weekly client-support volume with an AI platform, but that study is a working paper using one vendor's adopter clients, not peer-reviewed evidence (https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161)
opportunities.agent_design: A retrieval-grounded assistant with two surfaces and no free-form generation outside its sources. (1) Internal surface: staff ask 'what does SSAE 18 require for a complementary user entity control' or 'what did we request from this client last year' and get an answer with the source document and paragraph, drawn from the firm's own SOPs, checklists, engagement templates and prior-year workpapers. (2) Client-facing surface behind the portal login: answers only from the firm's published content library plus that client's own document checklist and engagement status ('your 1120 is waiting on two bank statements'), with a hard handoff to a person on anything involving advice, a deadline promise, or a number on a return. Every answer logs its sources; unanswered questions become a weekly content gap list the firm can feed back into its library. Human approval: the answer set and canned escalation wording are reviewed by a principal before go-live, and no client-facing answer can state a tax position.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: A generic assistant answering tax questions unsupervised is a liability under Circular 230 and the firm's own confidentiality duties, and it will confidently invent rules for a multi-state estate return. Making it safe requires retrieval scoped to firm-approved documents, per-client data isolation so one client's status never leaks into another's answer, refusal and escalation logic, and citation logging for review - plus a client-facing surface behind authentication that a chatbot subscription does not provide. The value is in the grounding and the guardrails, not the model.

impact_estimate.range: $1,500-$6,000 per year of principal and staff time (roughly 30-100 hours), plus after-hours coverage that does not exist today
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assumes 2-5 hrs/week currently spent on repeat client and staff questions across 100-250 clients, concentrated January-April (~130-260 hrs/yr), and a conservative 20-40% deflection once answers are grounded and cited. Hours valued at $48-$62/hr (NJ accountant median $100,830/yr base plus burden) because most answers today come from a principal or senior. Does not assume revenue from better conversion; the 55% support-volume figure is from a working paper on one vendor's clients and is used only as a directional ceiling.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2-4 weeks: ingest the published content library plus 10-15 firm checklists and templates into a retrieval index; stand up an internal-only assistant for the two principals and any staff; log 50 real questions with answer quality and escalation rate; deliver a ranked list of the recurring questions worth automating next and a draft client-facing answer set for principal review.

lead_score.rationale: Pain (17/30): the signals are structural rather than stated - a two-principal firm with a single phone line, no online booking, no published hours, a principal's personal email as the public front door, two overlapping document portals and a compliance-heavy mix including SOC 1 Type 2 - so the workload concentration is inferred, not complained about. All available reviews are firm-curated testimonials, none newer than late 2022, and they praise responsiveness rather than flagging delay. Fit (17/20): capabilities A, C and D all map onto evidenced work (intake and document collection, firm-authored content, attest evidence); no physical/edge or inventory use case, and tax-data confidentiality under IRC Sec. 7216 and the FTC Safeguards Rule forces a vetted or private deployment, which trims the score. Ability to pay (14/20): a boutique practice with high-value assurance and valuation lines in a dense, high-wage county cluster (Middlesex NAICS 5412 average annual pay $149,231; metro accountant median $105,650), but headcount, revenue and fees are unknown and a 3-8 person firm has a real budget ceiling. Ease (10/15): the pilot can start on the public form and mailbox with a single portal, but there is no CRM, no exposed API contract for TaxDome confirmed in this session, and any client-data work needs a security review and consent handling before go-live. Strategic (14/15): this stack - static marketing site, TaxDome, QuickBooks, small attest practice - is close to the default configuration of thousands of small US CPA firms, so the same three builds resell with configuration rather than new engineering. Total 72/100; evidence_thin is set true because the pain case rests on site structure and inference rather than on any measured or stated client complaint.
lead_score.notes: Capability letter convention: A operational, B research/discovery, C knowledge, D agent-built custom software, E physical/edge, F AgentOps retainer.

best_evidence_signal: A two-principal firm routes every prospect through a plain POST-back form with no booking or stated response time, a single phone line, and the lead principal's own email - while its testimonials sell responsiveness as the differentiator: https://www.rizickcpas.com/consultation.htm
